prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms made optical frequency standards with uncertainty and stability near the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep B049 as my preferred configuration, with the credit limited to Katori and Ye. The scientific core has not changed through the exchange: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift on the clock transition so that many atoms can be interrogated together with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, and Ye's strontium work showed what that idea delivers, performance near 10^-18. The physics rests on atomic structure (differential polarizabilities, blackbody and higher-order lattice shifts, clock-transition properties) that Lindroth and I can examine from the inside, and the results have been confirmed by independent laboratories and species and by direct clock-to-clock comparisons over about two decades. The same chain gives millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and a concrete route to redefining the second. The round-1 exchange made me more careful about the wording of the citation, not about the choice: it should be centred on the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice, so that it does not read as a third prize for the comb and ion-control lineage. I also accept the chair's request that the specific stability and uncertainty numbers be checked against the published record before a final vote, because my own recollection of the record figures is not verified.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my position is the one that Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson press, namely that B009 opens a new class of quantum matter, whereas B049 is a decisive improvement in measurement in a lineage recognised in 2005 and 2012, and that its fundamental-physics results so far are null tests. I do not dismiss it. B009 has by far the broadest opening support, a very clean prediction-then-observation chain, and I ranked it last mainly because it lies outside my specialty, which is a limitation of my judgement and not evidence about the physics. For B049 itself, the redefinition of the second has not happened, Lemonde, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups have arguable claims to parts of the story, and a two-name award will be criticised for omissions however it is worded. The record-accuracy figures supplied in the candidate file need independent checking.

responses.point: Distinguishes the discovery of flat bands and correlated states in magic-angle graphene from the still-open interpretation, and argues that the unsettled pairing mechanism does not make B009 premature, since earlier prizes honoured established phenomena of unsettled microscopic origin.
responses.response: This is a fair distinction and it moves me partly. I agree that a prize for the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the predicted angle would not need a settled mechanism, and the precedent is real. Where I still differ is on timing and not on kind: about eight years after the key experiments, the phase diagram, the role of strain and twist-angle disorder and the origin of the superconductivity are all still moving, and a citation on those states may need reinterpretation as they are understood. I also note that your own answer to my credit-spread point, the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction plus the Jarillo-Herrero observation as the decisive contributions, concedes that Cao, Dean, Young and Yacoby are outside the award. That does not defeat B009, but it is a real attribution cost that B049 does not carry. I therefore keep B009 as my first alternative and would not obstruct it.

responses.point: Argues that twisted bilayer graphene opens a new area of physics instead of refining a measurement, that outside-specialty ranking should not outweigh breadth of adoption, and says he would support B049 if the committee wanted a metrology prize but not above B009.
responses.response: I accept the point that my eighth place for B009 reflects my own limits and should not be read as a scientific verdict, and I am glad that we agree on the quality of both candidates. I disagree with the framing of B049 as only a refinement of measurement. The lattice clock is a new physical regime, a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which is the reason the stability is so much better than for single-ion clocks, and it has already given gravitational redshift over millimetres inside one sample. Measuring something an order of magnitude better, with a new method that opens new tests, is the pattern of the precision-measurement prizes. The disagreement between us is therefore about weighting new matter against new capability to measure, which the statutes do not decide, and I would not claim that the clock side wins that weighing; I only claim it is a legitimate weighing.

responses.point: Moved off circuit QED after the 2025 prize and the omission of Girvin and Devoret, and now prefers B012 with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, while asking whether lattice clocks are a discovery or an improvement in measurement and ranking them below B012.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved off B040 for the reasons I gave, and I agree that the same timing logic applies to the 2025 circuit prize. On B012 I still see the science as excellent, but the credit problem remains unresolved. With Zoller, Cirac, Greiner and Bloch on a four-name list, Jaksch outside it, and Esslinger, Haensch and Bakr with arguable claims, any three names would be contested, and the topic sits close to the 2001 condensate prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems. I cannot say the analogue-simulation payoff is delivered either. On your question whether B049 is a discovery, my answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is an invention in the Nobel sense and the 10^-18 demonstration is its realisation; the prize rewards both. I keep B012 as a second alternative, and I would need a convincing division of the theory credit before moving it higher.

responses.point: Asks that the specific stability and uncertainty numbers behind the 10^-18 claim be checked rather than taken from general knowledge, and notes that his chair summary lists whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second as an open question.
responses.response: You are right that the accuracy figures are the weakest part of my argument as written, and I withdraw any reliance on my memory of them. The committee should verify three things before the vote: the systematic uncertainty and instability reported for the JILA strontium clock, the independent lattice-clock results from other laboratories (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN) with direct comparisons, and Katori's original magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice-clock spectroscopy. On waiting for the redefinition of the second, I would not make it a condition. The discovery is the lattice clock and its performance, which is established, whereas the redefinition is an administrative step of the metrology bodies that depends on timing and on more than one clock species. I would also apply an equal standard to both leading candidates, as the chair's question asks: if an unresolved mechanism is not a bar for B009, an unfinished redefinition is not a bar for B049.

responses.point: Accepts that B049 is a natural two-person prize with twenty years of confirmation, but argues that the clocks refine precision measurement, with close precedent in 2005 and 2012, and lists B049 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Your point about precedent is the argument I take most seriously against my own position, and I would not call it answered by assertion. What I can say is that the 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize recognised the control and measurement of single quantum systems; neither recognised the use of an engineered optical lattice to cancel the clock shift for thousands of atoms, which is Katori's idea. That is why I want the citation drafted around that concept. Since you rank B049 first among your alternatives, the real question may be how the committee wants to weigh B009 against it, and I suggest the vote should be allowed to decide that and not an attempt to find a compromise.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize once the citation is centred on the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice.
Whether a third name such as Lemonde or Ludlow is warranted, or whether Katori and Ye is defensible against the PTB, NIST and SYRTE claims; I have not verified the priority record independently.
The exact record stability and uncertainty figures for lattice clocks, which I have not verified and which the committee should check.

How much weight the unsettled pairing mechanism in B009 should carry compared with its rapid reproduction and the clean prediction-then-observation chain, and whether I am applying an equal maturity standard to B009 and B049.
Whether my own specialist closeness to the field of precision atomic spectroscopy leads me to overrate B049 relative to B009, which I cannot assess in the same detail.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. For B049 I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is linked to the JILA precision-spectroscopy environment in which Jun Ye works; I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. No colleague has said this requires recusal, but I leave the decision to the committee and would accept a decision to recuse myself from the final vote on B049 or to have my view weighed accordingly. As a Lund atomic physicist I am also professionally close to the precision-spectroscopy field, which I have flagged as a possible bias. For B012 my European quantum-memory collaborations overlap with the community around Cirac and Zoller, and for B040 I have been involved in WACQT; neither candidate is in my preferred configuration. I report no new connection since round 1.
